method: Each listed item was read with its stem, all options, keyed answer(s), explanations and takeaway. Statuses are manually reasoned, not inferred from a schema or automated pass rule.
limitations: Independent AI editorial/clinical-reasoning screen; not external clinician validation or psychometric validation.
Pass applies only to the recorded content hash. New or changed content requires further review.
No comparison against proprietary examination items; originality judged from author provenance and item content.
Cross-bank learning-objective overlap remains provisional until all batches are available.
Source checks below support only the explicitly associated claims; other category references are general reading unless specifically verified.

options: Use the package’s serving size to decide whether it fits the plan
Review whether potassium chloride is an ingredient with the renal team
Continue using it while symptoms of high potassium are absent
Use the last normal potassium result as clearance for regular use
why: Serving size alone does not establish potassium content or fit with the prescribed restriction.
Some low-sodium substitutes contain potassium chloride and need review against the renal plan.
Important potassium elevation may occur without reliable warning symptoms.
A prior normal result does not establish safety of a new regular potassium source.

items.assessment: Key now includes immediate responsiveness/airway/breathing assessment and urgent review rather than a communication-only response. New arousal decline must not be normalized as evening fatigue.
Unusual prolonged unresponsiveness differs from the known post-seizure pattern; key explicitly assesses airway/breathing/responsiveness with urgent review. No unsafe oral administration remains.
The stem limits focus to bleeding extent and injury exposure. Trauma and other bleeding sites fit; meal timing and one old bruise’s colour do not assess that new pattern.
New functional decline/cough/poor intake warrant acute-illness assessment without requiring fever. Supplements and cough suppression alone are plausible premature symptom management.
Direct positional symptoms and measured change best describe the event. Medication timing/glucose/history are relevant accompanying context but do not substitute for observed response.
Current mental-status/abdominal trends identify deterioration; stable old veins/oedema are now parallel baseline comparators. No competing acute key remains.
Symptomatic high ileostomy losses warrant hydration assessment/team contact; plain-water escalation with delay may not address electrolyte needs and larger pouch only changes containment.
Severe pain/vomiting/no flatus require urgent obstruction review before routine laxative or diet treatment. Antiemetic relief must not postpone assessment.
All alternatives now interpret the old screen against new clinical evidence. Later cough/weight loss justify swallowing reassessment; screening is not permanent clearance.
Inspecting the symptomatic device contact area takes precedence over reassuring global score or adding unassessed padding. Necessary oxygen therapy is no longer presented as stopped indefinitely.
New palpitations after unexplained syncope need reassessment/escalation despite transient recovery. Routine rest/recheck or anxiety attribution are relevant premature closure errors.
